# Pre-installed tools — what every computer ships with

Every Hoody computer starts as a **Debian/Ubuntu base** with a curated battery of dev tools already on `$PATH`. **Computers run real systemd as PID 1 with root inside the computer** — not a Docker-style minimal sandbox. That means `systemctl`, `journalctl`, `apt install <package> && systemctl enable --now <unit>`, `crontab -e`, drop-in unit overrides and socket activation work as on a normal distro. Computers share the host kernel, so computer root cannot load kernel modules. Two tiers of pre-installed software:

1. **Default tier** — installed when the computer's resolved `hoody_kit` setting is true. Left out of `hoody computers create`, it is true for a login (JWT) caller; for an auth-token caller it follows the token's `computers.features.hoody_kit` permission, so it is false when the token lacks it. A computer with `hoody_kit` false is not guaranteed to have these packages.
2. **`dev_kit: true`** — the comprehensive coding setup (Node 26, Bun, Rust, Go, Nix, Docker, …). Pass it on `hoody computers create`, or the `--dev-kit` flag; when omitted, `dev_kit` defaults to the resolved `hoody_kit` value.

Anything missing? Just `apt install`, `npm i -g`, `cargo install`, `go install`, `nix-env -i`, etc. — root is yours, the box is yours. The system Python is externally managed (PEP 668), so a bare `pip install` is refused: use a virtual environment for libraries and `pipx install` for Python CLIs. The `dev_kit` installer attempts to install `python3-venv` and `pipx`; if either is missing, run `sudo apt install python3-venv pipx`

## `kvm: true` — run full VMs inside the computer

Computers on **dedicated (bare-metal) servers** can enable `/dev/kvm` passthrough and run hardware-accelerated virtual machines (QEMU/KVM, libvirt, Firecracker, …) inside the computer. Pass `kvm: true` on `hoody computers create`, or the `--kvm` flag, or toggle it later on a **stopped** computer (`hoody computers kvm enable -c <computer-id>` / `hoody computers kvm disable -c <computer-id>`). Defaults to off. **Never available on free-tier servers or paid subservers (slices)**: the API refuses with `403`. An auth token also needs the `computers.features.kvm` permission (otherwise `403`). `dev_kvm` is accepted as an input alias of `kvm` (`kvm` wins; if both are sent they must agree). Every computer response carries the current `kvm` boolean. A create with KVM requested can still come back `kvm: false` with a `kvm_note` (KVM was not enabled automatically, so the computer was created with KVM off): check both `kvm` and `kvm_note` in the answer, and if it is off, enable it with the toggle once the computer is stopped.

```bash
PROJECT_ID="<project-id>"; SERVER_ID="<server-id>"; COMPUTER_ID="<computer-id>"
hoody computers create --project "$PROJECT_ID" --server-id "$SERVER_ID" --name vm-host --kvm -o json   # enable at creation; check kvm / kvm_note in the output
hoody computers kvm enable -c "$COMPUTER_ID"    # enable on a stopped computer
hoody computers kvm disable -c "$COMPUTER_ID"   # disable
```

## `hoody` CLI is pre-installed inside every computer

The `hoody` binary is on every computer's `$PATH` (`/usr/bin/hoody`) for root, the default `user` account and any account that holds `user`'s group — from a shell session, an `exec` script, a `daemon` program, a cron entry or an SSH session running as one of them. Other uids cannot run it: the binary lives under `/hoody`, which only root and that group can enter; give such a uid its own install of the CLI.

```bash
hoody --version
hoody projects list
hoody --computer <computerId> files get /home/user
```

Do not assume that a shell or program inside the computer has a default computer id. When a command needs one, pass `--computer <computerId>` or set `HOODY_COMPUTER=<computerId>`. The CLI checks `HOODY_COMPUTER`, then `HOODY_COMPUTER_ID`, then the older `HOODY_CONTAINER` and `HOODY_CONTAINER_ID`. Whether a terminal session or a `daemon` program receives these variables depends on its environment injection settings and on what environment is available to it; a cron job can set them in its crontab. Hoody Agent shells can receive the computer bound to the agent session. `$HOODY_TOKEN` is not set in ordinary terminal, `exec`, `daemon` or cron processes: give that code a token through its own environment (a script's `.env`, the program's env) if it needs to call the API. Hoody Agent shells can be the exception: with the agent's Hoody integration on and a usable credential, the agent injects `HOODY_TOKEN` and the API base URL into its bash tool (for a realm session normally a minted realm token; some installs fall back to the account token, and a failed mint or a restricted login injects nothing). Login state is per-user under `~/.hoody/config.json`.

This is the same binary as `hoody` outside the computer, so the CLI skill's examples work the same way inside a computer's shell, once that environment has the sign-in and the `--computer` target an example needs.

## Default user — `user` (uid 1000) with passwordless sudo

Computers created with the Hoody Kit (`hoody_kit: true`) ship with a **non-root account named `user`** (uid 1000, gid 1000, member of `sudo`). Home is `/home/user`. **`/etc/sudoers.d/user` grants `user ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL`** — passwordless `sudo` lets agents (and humans) escalate to root for any operation without prompting.

The Hoody Agent runs as `user` and its shell follows this setting: with the drop-in in place the agent can sudo; once the drop-in is removed (or narrowed to some commands) the agent's shell gets exactly what `user` gets without a password.

**Use `user` for everyday work, sudo when you actually need root.** Reasons:

- Files created under `user` are owned by uid 1000 — friendlier when you copy/sync them out of the computer or back-stop with rsync.
- Many apps (npm, pip in venvs, Bun, Go, Nix single-user, Docker rootless, browsers) write into `$HOME` and behave better when `$HOME` is a real user home, not `/root`. (The Rust toolchain is shared: it lives under `/usr/local/cargo` and `/usr/local/rustup`, not under `$HOME`.)
- `journalctl --user`, `systemctl --user`, dbus user buses all hang off a regular user.

The kit's `terminal` / `daemon` / `cron` namespaces let you pass `user: 'user'` (default in many surfaces is `root` — be explicit). Examples: `hoody daemon programs create --name my-app --command '…' --user user`, `hoody terminal sessions create --terminal-id 100 --user user --shell bash --cwd /home/user` (`terminal_id` may be omitted when the `terminal-N` host supplies it, or when `ephemeral: true` generates it. On a computer-scoped client the SDK takes the host index from the body id; if you also pass `serviceIndex`, it must be the same id, or the SDK throws a `ValidationError` before sending. A request that reaches the kit with a mismatched id is refused with `400 TERMINAL_ID_MISMATCH`. The `terminal-0` host creates only ephemeral sessions). The generated `GET /{path}` (HTTP only; no CLI command) does NOT take a `user` param — the script runs under whatever uid the kit was started as.

**Production hardening — disable passwordless sudo.** For computers exposed to untrusted callers (open kit URLs without proxy gates, public alias hostnames, agents you don't fully trust), revoke the NOPASSWD line:

```bash
sudo passwd user && sudo rm /etc/sudoers.d/user    # set a real password first (the account may have none), then remove the drop-in only if that worked
```

Or replace the contents with a tighter policy (e.g. `user ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart myapp` for one specific command). Edit via `sudo visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/user` to validate syntax before commit. Reminder: a leaked kit URL is already a root-shell credential (see auth-model — capability-token semantics); production exposure should ALSO have `hoody computers proxy permissions *` and `hoody computers proxy groups *` gates and ideally a non-root default user.

## Default tier — with `hoody_kit`

### Network & download
`curl`, `wget`, `net-tools` (`ifconfig`/`netstat`), `dnsutils` (`dig`/`nslookup`), `traceroute`, `socat`, `ncat`, `gpg`, `screen`, `rsync`, `sshpass`.

### Shell & terminal
`bash` (default), `zsh`, `fish`, `tmux`, `nano`, `xterm`, `psmisc`, `coreutils`, `lsof`, `bc`, `tree`, `fuse3`.

### Search / parse / archive
`ripgrep` (`rg`), `jq`, `yq`, `unzip`, `rar`.

### X11 helpers
`xsel`, `xclip`, `wmctrl`, `xdotool` — drive any GUI from the shell, pair with the `display` kit.

### Version control
`git`.

### Database
`sqlite3`.

### Scheduler
`cron`.

### Build toolchain
`build-essential`, `gcc`, `g++`, `make`, `cmake`, `autoconf`, `automake`, `pkg-config`, `bison`, `flex`, `libtool`, `gettext`.

### Python (for scripts)
`python3` (system), `python3-dev`, `python3-pip`, `python3-setuptools`, plus dev bindings for cairo / GTK / dbus / cryptography / Pillow / paramiko / netifaces.

### System dev libs (headers, for compiling against)
`libssl-dev`, `libffi-dev`, `libcairo2-dev`, `libgtk-3-dev`, `libglib2.0-dev`, `libpango1.0-dev`, `libncurses-dev`, X11 dev libs (`libx11-dev`, `libxrandr-dev`, `libxext-dev`, `libxtst-dev`, …), OpenGL (`libgl1-mesa-dev`), media codecs (`libjpeg`, `libpng`, `libwebp`, `libavcodec`, `libx264`, `libvpx`, `libaom`), GStreamer.

## `dev_kit: true` tier — comprehensive coding setup

Set the flag on `hoody computers create` to additionally provision:

### JavaScript / TypeScript
- **Node.js 26** (system-wide via NodeSource — not nvm).
- **Bun** (system-wide).
- **Yarn + pnpm** (via Corepack).
- **npm globals**: `typescript`, `ts-node`, `tsx`, `@types/node`, `eslint`, `prettier`, `@biomejs/biome`, `npm-check-updates`, `nodemon`, `concurrently`.

### Python
- **pipx** (isolated CLI installs).

### Compiled languages
- **Rust** + **cargo** (system rustup).
- **Go** (latest).

### Package managers
- **Nix** (multi-user daemon install, falling back to single-user if that fails) — declarative installs without touching apt.
- **pkgx** — runs CLIs without installing them globally.

### Containers (Docker)
- **Docker Engine** + **buildx** + **compose plugin** + **containerd**.

### CLI utilities
`shellcheck`, `direnv`, `httpie`, `fd-find` (aliased as `fd`), `bat`, `fzf`, `gh` (GitHub CLI).

### AI agent CLIs (installed by default)
- **Claude Code** (`claude`, npm `@anthropic-ai/claude-code`)
- **Codex** (`codex`, npm `@openai/codex`)
- **opencode** (`opencode`, npm `opencode-ai`)
- **Gemini CLI** (`gemini`, npm `@google/gemini-cli`)

Installed without credentials.

## How to add more

```bash
# As root; as `user` (passwordless sudo), prefix the system-wide installs with sudo
# Anything Debian-packaged
apt-get install -y jq

# Python (install python3-venv and pipx if missing)
pipx install httpie

# Node global
npm i -g typescript

# Rust (only if dev_kit installed; installs into the caller's own CARGO_HOME, which must be writable)
cargo install ripgrep

# Go (only if dev_kit installed)
go install golang.org/x/tools/gopls@latest

# Nix (only if dev_kit installed) — best for one-off binaries that bring 30 deps
nix-env -iA nixpkgs.hello
```

State is per-computer: `hoody computers copy` clones the disk including everything you installed; `hoody snapshots create` saves a point-in-time you can later `hoody snapshots restore` to roll back to. There is no global "shared layer" leak — each computer's filesystem is its own.

# CLI — Core operations

Use the `hoody` CLI only where it is already installed: a Hoody computer, or the user's own computer. In a web chat (ChatGPT, claude.ai, …) or a throwaway code sandbox, use HTTP instead: the CLI isn't installed there, a login made there does not last, and it isn't the user's machine. Do not install it with npx or the install script; check with `command -v hoody`.

`hoody` recipes. Base URL: `https://api.hoody.com` by default; override with `--base-url <url>`, `HOODY_BASE_URL` or `hoody config set baseUrl <url>`. Scope: `-c <cid>` | `HOODY_COMPUTER` | `hoody local defaults set computer <id>`.

---

### 1. Sign up
Default for a person: they sign up at `https://api.hoody.com/auth/signup` in their own browser, then sign in with `hoody login --web --no-browser` (§2). Existing account: always browser sign-in first; if it fails, stalls or is refused, ask for a token they create at `https://api.hoody.com/auth/home#/keys` (side menu → Keys and tokens → API keys). Never ask for a password (use one only if offered). Never repeat or store a secret. `hoody signup --email you@example.com --password "$HOODY_PASSWORD"` — signup, email verification and login in one command. On a TTY it waits for you to click the verification link and ends logged in; without a TTY it exits 0 after sending the verification email and you must run `hoody login` yourself once the link is clicked. Signup CLI flags are `--email`, `--password` (or `--password-stdin`), `[--region]`, `[--invite-code <code>]` (remembered as a hash at signup and, after email verification, attempted automatically when needed for gated provisioning; validity is not checked at signup), `[--print-token]` (needs a terminal: without a TTY the command exits 1 before it signs up), `[--no-save]`, `[--wait]` and `[--challenge <code>]` (the browser check, below); there is no `--username`; username is generated (usually from the email local part; log in with the email). Password 12–128 chars and at most 72 UTF-8 bytes. The server needs **3 of 4** character classes (upper/lower/digit/symbol); the interactive prompt demands all four, so use all four. Resend: `hoody auth email verification send --email <email>`. Signup may first ask a person to finish a short check in a browser. On a TTY the command shows the link and the match code and waits until the check passes. Without a TTY it creates nothing, prints the link, the match code and the command that carries on (`-o json`: `challenge_required`, `verification_url`, `match_code`, `challenge`, `next`, and `next_argv`, the same command as an argv array) and exits 2: show the person the link and code, and once they have finished run `next` with the same password on stdin (it keeps the email, `--region`, `--invite-code`, `--profile`, `--config`, `--realm`, `--base-url` and the output format, plus `--challenge <code>`; a `--base-url` with a query, fragment or user name and any `--proxy` are left out and `next_notes` asks for them; it exits 2 again while the check is not finished, or with a new link when a check did not pass). `--wait` keeps the command waiting instead (run it in the background and read the link from stderr). The check lasts about 15 minutes. A check that runs out exits 1: start again. When no answer ends the check (the wait runs out, or a `--challenge` run gets no answer) it also exits 1 (`-o json`: `outcome_unknown`), and the account may exist if the check was finished: check the email or run `hoody login`. Exit 0 means the signup was accepted, which is also the answer for an address that already has an account.

### 2. Log in (+2FA)
`hoody login --web --no-browser` is browser sign-in: it prints a link and a code for the user, polls until they approve on Hoody's page, and saves the session (2FA happens in their browser). If your shell tool shows output only after a command exits, run it in the background and read the link from its output. Password path (last resort, see the order in §1), or for a user signing in from their own terminal: `hoody login --username alex --password "$HOODY_PASSWORD"` (or `--email you@example.com`). On a TTY a 2FA account is prompted for its code in the same run. Without a TTY the command saves nothing, prints the challenge and exits 2; finish with `hoody auth 2fa verify --temp-token <temp_token> --code 123456` using the printed temp token (`--code` also accepts a 10-character backup code). Login password ≥8 chars (signup is ≥12).

### 3. Base URL / profiles
Global flags: `--base-url <URL>`, `--profile <P>`. Persist with `hoody config set baseUrl <URL>` (camelCase key).

### 4. List projects
`hoody projects list [-o json]`

### 5. Create project
`hoody projects create --alias my-project --color '#10B981'`

### 6. List computers
`hoody computers list [--realm <rid>] [-o wide]`. There is no `--project` filter. One call fetches every page, up to 10,000 items or 1,000 requests (`--limit N` caps the total; past the bound the CLI says so on stderr, and `--limit 100 --page 101` continues), so filter the result with `hoody computers list -o json | jq '.computers[] | select(.project_id=="<pid>")'` (the CLI's `-o json` unwraps the API envelope, so the top level is the `data` body — `.computers`, not `.data.items`). `--name <text>` keeps the computers whose name contains the text (case-insensitive). `hoody computers get <name>` also accepts an exact, case-sensitive name that matches exactly one computer; a 24-hex value is always read as an id, and an ambiguous name, or a lookup that hit the bound, is refused, so pass the id then.

### 7. Create computer
`hoody computers create --project <pid> --server-id <sid> --name box-1 --hoody-kit`. Flags `--project` and `--server-id` are required.
`<sid>` is the rental's `server_id`, not the ID column of `hoody servers list` (that is the rental id): `hoody servers list -o json | jq -r '.[].server_id'`. Rentable servers: `hoody servers marketplace list`. Rent with `hoody servers rent <id> --rental-days <days> --max-charge-cents <total-cents>`: pick a duration the server offers and convert `pricing.price_tiers[days].total_first_payment` to integer cents (`"37.00"` → `3700`; the total includes any setup fee); only a zero-total rental may omit `--max-charge-cents`, otherwise the call answers `409 CHARGE_CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED`, or `409 SETUP_FEE_CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED` when a setup fee applies.
After the computer is `running`, give the user the clickable URLs of its main kits (each opens its web UI): `hoody open terminal --url -c <cid>`, then the same with `notifications` (slug `n` in the URL), `desktop`, `browser`, `files` and `agent`. `--url` only prints; without it the command opens the page. See § 24.

### 8. Lifecycle — get/wait, start/stop/restart
```bash
CID=65a1f0c2e4b0a1b2c3d4e5f6   # your computer's 24-hex id, from hoody computers list
hoody computers get "$CID"
until [[ "$(hoody computers get "$CID" -o json|jq -r .status)" == running ]];do sleep 2;done   # CLI -o json unwraps the envelope → .status (not .data.status)
hoody computers restart "$CID"   # the same shape for start, stop, pause and resume; stop --force kills without a clean shutdown
```

### 9. One-off command
```bash
CID=65a1f0c2e4b0a1b2c3d4e5f6   # your computer's 24-hex id
hoody shell "$CID" -- ls -la /home/user   # the command is POSITIONAL — there is no --command flag
hoody shell "$CID" -- tmux ls
hoody terminal commands run --command 'ls' --ephemeral   # the flag form: `terminal commands run` takes the command in --command (hoody shell has no --command flag)
```

### 10. Long-lived terminal
```bash
hoody terminal sessions create --terminal-id 100 --shell bash
hoody terminal commands run --terminal-id 100 --command 'pwd' --wait
hoody terminal sessions read 100                  # terminal id optional, defaults to "1"
hoody terminal sessions snapshot get 100     # terminal id required
hoody terminal sessions delete 100 -y          # terminal id positional
```
Pin 1–1600 (new sessions take 1–9999 except the agent band (4501–5000 with the default bands), which is refused; with the default bands 1601–4500 = desktops, 4501–5000 = agents, 5001–7999 = ephemeral, 8001–9999 = Hoody Run/Hub).

### 11. SSH
`hoody shell <cid>` is not an SSH client by default; pass `--ssh-host`/`--ssh-user` to bridge to a real SSH server.

### 12. Files — list, read, write
```bash
hoody files get /home/user
hoody files stat /home/user/x
hoody files get /home/user/x --out-file /tmp/x   # byte for byte, text or binary
hoody files copy /home/user/x --copy-to /home/user/y
hoody files move /home/user/y --move-to /home/user/z
hoody files delete /home/user/z -y
hoody files upload /home/user/x --input /tmp/local.bin   # or pipe: cat f | hoody files upload /home/user/x
hoody files chunks write /home/user/x --input /tmp/more.bin   # appends raw bytes to an EXISTING file; `files upload --append` creates a missing one
```

### 13. Browser screenshot
`hoody browser screenshots capture --browser-id 1 --url https://example.com --format png --out-file /tmp/p.png`. The CLI uses `--browser-id` to pick the instance's `browser-N` host (the server checks any `browser_id` you send against that instance and answers `400 INSTANCE_SELECTOR_CONFLICT` on a mismatch); without it the CLI targets instance 1. Without `--out-file` the image bytes go to stdout as received (a terminal refuses them; redirect or pipe).

### 14. Display capture
```bash
hoody display screenshots capture --out-file /tmp/d.png      # take one now; or > /tmp/d.png: PNG bytes on stdout
hoody display screenshots latest get --out-file /tmp/d.png   # the most recent one already taken
# `hoody display thumbnails capture` / `thumbnails latest get` are the small versions; both take only `--base64`, `--display-id` and `--out-file`
```

### 15. SQLite KV
Key is positional; `--db <path>` is required; the JSON-encoded value goes in `--body`. The batch pair is typed instead: `--items` takes the item array as one JSON document (`--items @<file>.json` from a file, `--items @-` from standard input, or the array inline) or one `--items key=…,value=…,ttl=…` per item (`value` stays a string; do not mix the two forms). A batch value is stored as the text you give, not decoded as JSON: it is saved as `application/octet-stream` unless the item sets `content_type` (for example `content_type=application/json` to store a JSON value), and `--keys` takes the key list.
```bash
hoody kv set greeting --db /hoody/databases/app.db --body '"hello"' --create-db-if-missing       # value is a JSON-encoded string
hoody kv get greeting --db /hoody/databases/app.db
hoody kv set visits --db /hoody/databases/app.db --body '0'     # a counter holds a JSON number; increment on a non-number value is 400
hoody kv increment visits --db /hoody/databases/app.db --delta 1
hoody kv decrement visits --db /hoody/databases/app.db
echo '[{"key":"a","value":"v1"}]' > items.json
hoody kv batch set --db /hoody/databases/app.db --items @items.json
hoody kv batch set --db /hoody/databases/app.db --items 'key=a,value=v1' --items 'key=b,value=v2,ttl=60'
hoody kv batch get --db /hoody/databases/app.db --keys a,b
```

### 16. Watch — create + stream
`hoody watch create --paths /data --recursive` (`--paths` is repeatable; there is no `--name`). Then `hoody watch {list|events stream <id> -o ndjson}`.

### 17. Tunnels
`hoody tunnel {list|sessions list|bindings list|expose ...}`.

### 18. Snapshots
`hoody snapshots create --computer <cid> --alias pre-deploy [--expiry 30]`. Then `hoody snapshots {list | restore <name> | delete <name> | alias set <name> --alias <new>}` — each takes `--computer <cid>` (or `-c`) for the computer; `restore`, `delete` and `alias set` also take the snapshot name as a positional. `<name>` is the name `snapshots list` returns: the sanitized alias, or `snap-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS` when none was given. On `alias set`, the new alias goes in `--alias`.

### 19. Vault
```bash
hoody vault set api-token --value "$API_TOKEN"
hoody vault list
TOKEN=$(hoody vault get api-token -o json | jq -r .value)   # -o raw prints the whole JSON record, not the value
hoody vault delete api-token -y
hoody vault clear --yes   # deletes every key in the current realm (the account-level partition when none is selected); other realms keep theirs
```

### 20. Wallet balance
`hoody wallet balances general get` (general balance), `hoody wallet credits get` (AI credits), `hoody wallet balances get` (both). All three are refused for a token limited to realms (403 `REALM_TOKEN_ACCOUNT_MONEY`); use a login session or an unrestricted token.

### 21. Cron entries
```bash
hoody cron entries create user --schedule '0 */6 * * *' --command '/x.sh' --name b6   # the system user is positional and required
hoody cron entries list user
ID=$(hoody cron entries list user -o json | jq -r '.entries[] | select(.name=="b6") | .id')
hoody cron entries update user "$ID" --schedule '0 3 * * *'
hoody cron entries delete user "$ID" -y
hoody cron crontabs set user --crontab '0 3 * * * /x.sh'   # bulk: replaces the user's whole crontab
```

### 22. Daemon — supervised programs
```bash
hoody daemon programs create --id 100 --name app --command 'node /app/s.js' \
  --user user --boot --autorestart unexpected     # --boot (not --autostart) toggles auto-start at computer boot
hoody daemon programs list
hoody daemon programs logs get 100 --lines 200    # stop, logs get and logs stream take the numeric id as a positional, not --name
hoody daemon programs logs stream 100
hoody daemon programs stop 100
```

### 23. Exec — serverless script
```bash
hoody exec scripts write api/users.ts --create-dirs --validate \
  --content '// @mode serverless
return { users: [{ id: 1, name: "Alice" }] };'
```
`// @mode {serverless|worker}`; return value or `module.exports = async(req,res,meta,shared)=>…`.

### 24. Open kit in browser
```bash
hoody open terminal   # service ∈ agent|browser|code|cron|db|desktop|display|exec|files|kv|notes|notifications|pipe|run|terminal|watch|sqlite|curl|logs|ssh|egress|http|https|http-<port>|https-<port>. Top-level `open` takes a service name, NOT a computer id.
hoody files open   # the kit's own open; display, code, exec, db, kv and notifications have one too
```

### 25. Ask Hoody about Hoody (docs chatbot)
`hoody chat ['prompt']`: a one-shot question, or an interactive REPL when the prompt is omitted. Hoody's hosted docs assistant answers questions about Hoody with no API key; use `hoody agent prompt` for agentic AI. In the REPL, `--persist` saves sessions and `--persist --resume [id]` resumes the latest or a given one; `--private` disables disk reads and writes.

### 26. Discover kits
`hoody kits list [--named-only]` — kit slug catalog; see § Proxy URLs above.

### 27. Debug flags
```bash
hoody projects list --verbose         # show HTTP req/resp
hoody projects list --quiet           # drops helper chatter; -o json/yaml/raw output still printed
hoody exec namespaces list --refresh-scripts
hoody files get /x -o raw | bash      # -o raw drops envelope
```

### 28. Structured (JSON) flags
A flag whose `--help` shows `<json|@file.json|@->` takes one JSON document, from any of three sources with the same result: inline, from a file (`@file.json`) or from standard input (`@-`). Only one flag of a command can read standard input. Malformed JSON, or an array where an object is expected, is refused before anything is sent. `<value|json|@file.json|@->` also takes a scalar, and its help lists the JSON types the field takes: inline text is read as JSON first (`true`, `42`, `null`, `'"x"'` the string x), and text that is not JSON (a plain token) is sent as a string when the field takes one. A `<key=value>` flag (a map, or a list such as `kv batch set --items`) takes KEY=VALUE entries or the whole value as one JSON document, never both and never two documents; a token starting with `@` is always a file (or `@-`), so a key cannot start with `@`, `{` or `[`.
```bash
hoody agent settings update --patch '{"model":null}'
hoody agent workflows set --name check --definition @workflow.json
printf '%s\n' '{"model":null}' | hoody agent settings update --patch @-
```

URLs → § Proxy URLs; auth → § Auth model; per-namespace flags → `SKILL-CLI/<ns>.md`.

# CLI — Reference appendix

## Global flags

|Flag|Notes|
|---|---|
|`-o`|`json`/`yaml`/`table`/`wide`/`raw`/`ndjson`/`pretty` (none typed and none saved: a fixed human layout on a terminal, the plain `table` layout on a pipe, with `TERM=dumb`, in CI or in agent mode)|
|`-q`,`-v`,`--no-color`|suppress helper chatter (status/side messages — JSON/YAML/raw output still emitted); HTTP req/resp; no color|
|`--config`,`--profile`|`~/.hoody/config.json`|
|`--base-url`|API base URL for this run (default `https://api.hoody.com`; also `HOODY_BASE_URL` or `hoody config set baseUrl <url>`).|
|`-t`,`-u`,`-p`,`-y`|bearer; login identifier (username, or an email: a value containing `@` is sent as `email`); pw; auto-yes|
|`-c`,`--realm`,`--proxy`,`--non-interactive`|computer(→env); realm; proxy; CI|
|`--domain`|update-verify; **precede subcommand**|
|`--kit-*`|kit auth; capability URL is credential|
|`--local-password*`,`--local-lock-timeout`,`--allow-ephemeral-token`,`--refresh-scripts`|lock+cache|

Status: in the human layout, status glyphs are green for running, cyan for starting and red for error; stopped and paused glyphs are unpainted, and status words are unpainted. In the plain table layout, stopped and paused status values are yellow when color is enabled.

## Output formats

With no explicit `-o` and no saved machine format, a normal terminal gets the human layout; a pipe, `TERM=dumb`, CI or agent mode (`HOODY_AGENT_MODE=1`) gets the plain layout, and typing `-o table` or `-o wide` also selects the plain layout. A saved `json`, `yaml`, `ndjson` or `raw` format takes precedence when no `-o` is typed. `json`/`yaml` print just the unwrapped `data` payload (the CLI strips the `{statusCode,message,data}` envelope via `isApiEnvelope`), except on a command whose answer has fields beside `data` (the `hoody boturls` management and key commands, for one, with `propagation`): those print `{ data, … }`, so read `.data.<field>` there; with `--until-done`, `-o json` prints `{ response: <that payload>, outcome: { state, event } }` instead (`state` is `done`, `failed`, `timeout`, `interrupted` or `unauthorized`), and `-o yaml` is unchanged; `raw`=payload/SSE; when piped, in CI or in agent mode, generated event streams and `events stream` print `ndjson`, while `proxy logs stream` and `pipe progress stream` print readable lines unless you type `-o ndjson` or `-o json` (`hoody agent prompt` defaults to `pretty` on a terminal, `ndjson` when piped); `pretty`=human stream. `-q` keeps `json`/`yaml`.

## Exit codes

`0`=success; `1`=general command/HTTP failure (4xx and 5xx both, except as `4` and `124` below and in `hoody exec remote`); `2`=a usage refusal of the CLI's own (a missing or malformed Bot URL key or URL, a Bot URL caller's parser error, `--http` or `--http-curl` on a command that has neither, a retired flag spelling, some `hoody shell` errors, an unknown `--profile` on `logout`), a pending 2FA challenge (login saved nothing; finish with `hoody auth 2fa verify --temp-token …`), a signup that needs a browser check (nothing created; finish the check, then run the printed `hoody signup … --challenge <code>`), an update failure, or an exec-dynamic parse failure (other parser errors, such as an unknown option, generally exit `1`); `3`=authenticated but saving credentials failed (or logout could not clear them, or `--print-token` had no token), or a history gap before a match in `events stream --once`; `4`=`events stream`, `computers wait` or `--until-done`: authorization failure (HTTP 401/403) or revocation; `6`=TTY absent (interactive prompt requested but no TTY available); `7`=in `hoody local lock`: a confirmation you declined or could not give (no terminal and no confirming flag), or multiple lock-password sources (everywhere else a declined confirmation prompt prints `Action cancelled` and exits `0`); `8`=lock contention; `9`=lock validation error; `10`=local-lock password or recovery rollback error, or a missing profile or field in `local lock reveal` (an unknown `--profile` on an ordinary command exits `1`); `11`=crypto/lock error; `12`=migration error; `14`=ephemeral-token policy; `70`=`hoody run` or a one-shot `hoody shell <id> -- <command>`: the server answered 5xx (for the shell, also an answer it could not read); `124`=the `--timeout` of `events stream`, `computers wait` or `--until-done` passed; `129`=SIGHUP; `130`=SIGINT; `143`=SIGTERM; `149`=SIGBREAK (Windows). `hoody exec remote` has its own codes: `3`=a disabled capability or a token without the scope (HTTP 403), `4`=a missing, invalid or non-eval token, `5`=the script threw (HTTP 422), `124`=timeout; `hoody exec remote --help` lists them. `hoody run --open`, `hoody run close` and `hoody run status` have theirs too: `2`=failed (nothing running, or the app exited non-zero) or a usage error, `3`=unknown or unreachable, `4`=a kit on the computer is too old to open apps (nothing was sent). A one-shot `hoody shell <id> -- <command>` exits with the command's own code, `124` on a timeout and `128`+N when a signal ended it. Two cases exit differently by command today: "No computer specified" exits `2` in `hoody agent`, `shell`, `daemon attach`, `share`, `run` and `voice`, and `1` in the kit commands, `egress local start`, `tunnel` and `pipe`; over the SSH gateway a refused `share`, `mount` or `unmount` exits `2`, and a refused `pipe`, `tunnel` or `egress local start` operation exits `1`.

## Login flow

`hoody login --web` is browser sign-in (add `--no-browser` to print the link and code instead of opening a browser); it polls until the user approves and saves the session. The rest of this section is the password path: `POST /api/v1/users/auth/login`. Auto-login from the global `-u`/`--username` (or `HOODY_USERNAME`/config) sends a value containing `@` as `email` and anything else as `username`. The explicit `hoody login` sends exactly the flag you pass: `--username <name>` or `--email <addr>`. If the response carries a `temp_token` without a `token`, the auto-login flow throws `Auto-login cannot complete the 2FA challenge`; finish the flow explicitly with `hoody auth 2fa verify --temp-token <tt> --code <6-digit OTP or 10-char backup code>` (or call `POST /api/v1/users/auth/2fa/verify`). Token persisted; `hoody logout` clears.

## Local-only operations

`hoody local` — `~/.hoody/`, no server calls. `defaults set <key> <value>` pins `computer`/`realm`/`output`/`noColor`/`quiet`, `defaults get` shows them and `defaults clear <key>` removes one. `lock {enable|status|password set|reveal|disable|ephemeral enable|ephemeral disable|recover|doctor|delete}` (no `unlock` subcommand) uses `flock()`. `--non-interactive` accepts exactly one password source: `--local-password <pw>`, `HOODY_LOCAL_PASSWORD` env var, file/fd, or stdin. Combining sources (an env var plus a flag included) is refused with exit code 7.

## Update

Two channels. With an update domain (`--domain`/`HOODY_DOMAIN`/`~/.config/hoody/domain`) the CLI fetches that domain's manifest and **minisign-verifies** it against the build-embedded key (bad sig aborts; an explicit but untrusted domain is refused, never downgraded). With no domain configured (the npm and install-script default) it asks npm, then GitHub, for the latest version: no signature check. `update` checks for newer releases and prints install instructions; it does not atomically replace `$0`. The update banner runs only on bare `hoody`, `--help`, and explicit `hoody update` (no per-command implicit check). `HOODY_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1` suppresses the banner.

## Environment variables

`HOODY_TOKEN`/`HOODY_API_TOKEN`, `HOODY_COMPUTER`/`_ID`, `HOODY_REALM`/`_ID`, `HOODY_USERNAME`, `HOODY_PASSWORD`, `HOODY_BASE_URL`/`_API_URL`, `HOODY_PIPE_URL`, `HOODY_PROFILE`, `HOODY_DOMAIN`, `HOODY_KIT_AUTH`, `HOODY_KIT_USER`, `HOODY_KIT_TOKEN`, `HOODY_KIT_TOKEN_HEADER`, `HOODY_KIT_PASSWORD`, `HOODY_NO_UPDATE_CHECK`, `NO_COLOR`, proxy (`ALL_PROXY`/`HTTPS_PROXY`/`HTTP_PROXY`). The config file path is set via the global `--config` flag (no `HOODY_CONFIG` env var).

## Bot URLs

`hoody boturls` manages your Bot URLs by `bu_` id (`list`, `create`, `get`, `update`, `repoint`, `panic`, `delete`, `label suggest`, and the key commands `keys create <id> --name <name>`, `keys update <id> <key-id>`, `keys rotate <id> <key-id>` and `keys revoke <id> <key-id>` (`keys revoke <id> --all` revokes every key); a new or rotated key's secret is printed once). While Bot URLs are unavailable on the platform (switched off, or no usable Bot zone), `create`, `label suggest`, `repoint` and an `update --enabled` that turns a disabled URL on are refused (503 `BOTS_DISABLED`); while the zone is missing, `url`, `test_curl` and the key's `curl` are `null` in JSON output and `-` in tables. The owner-side rules (who may manage one, the limits, labels, key handling, lifecycle and errors) are in the `api` namespace page, and the `agent` namespace page, Example 4, runs the whole flow: create, mint a key, call it, rotate, panic. The same group calls a Bot URL with a key and no `hoody login`: `hoody boturls ask <url> "<message>"`, `hoody boturls chat <url> "<message>"`, `hoody boturls status <url>`, `hoody boturls answer <url> --decision <decision>` with exactly one of `--gate-id <g_…>` or `--title <title>`, `hoody boturls models list <url>`, `hoody boturls updates list <url>` and `hoody boturls events stream <url>` (`events stream` follows the Bot live; it prints human-readable lines on a terminal's human layout and JSON lines otherwise, `-o json` (or `-o ndjson`) selects JSON lines, and `--max-wait <s>` takes whole seconds from 0 (no limit) to 86400, default 600). The key comes from `HOODY_BOT_KEY` (or the variable `--key-env` names) or `--key-file <path>` (`-` reads stdin); there is no `--key` flag, so the key never sits on a `hoody` command line. Set the variable without typing the key into a command (`read -rs HOODY_BOT_KEY && export HOODY_BOT_KEY`, then paste), or keep it in a file only you can read and pass `--key-file`; `export HOODY_BOT_KEY=hbk_…` typed in a shell puts the key in its history, and errors and diagnostics the Bot URL commands print contain no authentication material: they show fixed texts and checked fields only, a parser error (an unknown option, a missing argument) prints one fixed line that never repeats what you typed, the AI command fixer is never sent a command line with a token starting with `bot`, containing `.hoody.bot` or `hbk_`, or a `--key…` or `--zone` option (other command lines are sent as before, so never put a key in another command's arguments), and abort reasons are not propagated (what the Bot answers on success is printed as written, except that text output shows control and bidirectional-formatting characters as spaces; `-o json` prints it unchanged). Other global option checks can repeat the value they reject (an invalid `--realm`, for one), so pass the key only through `HOODY_BOT_KEY` (or the variable `--key-env` names) or `--key-file`, never as another option's value. `hoody boturls ask <url> "<message>"` follows the Bot's `working` refs for 600 seconds by default (`--max-wait <seconds>`; `--no-wait` does not wait) and can still end with `working` and exit code 0: without `-o json` the status and ref print on stderr, with `-o json` read `status` and `ref`, then rejoin with `hoody boturls ask <url> --ref <ref>` using the same key. A status that says it is waiting on a gate needs the owner. On `outcome_unknown` the Bot may already have acted: read `status <url>` or `updates list <url>` before sending again, because repeating the text can start new work. `hoody boturls chat` reads only the final message, which must be text only (at most 64 KiB); the Bot keeps its own conversation history. `hoody boturls answer <url> --gate-id <g_…> --decision <decision> [--text …]` (or `--title <title>` in place of `--gate-id` when the delegate has one pending gate; `<decision>` is one of `approve`, `allow_session`, `deny` or `answer`) answers a delegate's pending gate; a gate on the Bot's own session (`status` marks it owner-only) can only be resolved by the owner in the Hoody app. A caller verb given a `bu_` id points you at `get`; one given something that looks like a key refuses without repeating it. A refusal prints `<code>: <message>` with any `Retry-After` and the request ID and exits 1; a missing or malformed key or URL exits 2. `-o json` prints JSON (the old `--json` is refused, exit 2). The URL must be a label under `hoody.bot`, under the Bot zone of the platform the CLI was installed from, or under the zone `--zone <zone>` names; any other host is refused before the key is sent.

---

## Subskill index

Every namespace page is included below, in this order.

- `agent` — In-computer AI coding agent over HTTP
- `api` — Platform control plane: identity, projects, computers, billing, vault
- `browser` — Per-computer Chromium or Firefox instances, one per slot
- `code` — VS Code in the browser, per computer
- `cron` — managed crontab entries per system user
- `curl` — full HTTP client gateway + REST-as-GET-URL bridge
- `daemon` — supervisord program lifecycle (start any program; logs kept)
- `display` — programmatic GUI desktops with screenshots, input, and windows
- `egress` — the computer's outbound HTTP proxy
- `exec` — micro-services: any script or API as an instant HTTP endpoint
- `files` — computer filesystem over HTTP, with automatic Git-like change history
- `notes` — Collaborative notebooks, hierarchical nodes, documents, databases
- `notifications` — Trigger and consume desktop notifications inside a computer
- `pipe` — Zero-storage streaming HTTP transfers
- `proxyLogs` — Per-computer request/response/event log query, stats, and SSE tail
- `run` — resolve apps to shell commands
- `sqlite` — SQLite HTTP API
- `terminal` — Persistent multiplayer PTY sessions over HTTP and WebSocket
- `tunnel` — reverse tunnels for HTTP/WS/TCP via computer relay
- `vm` — virtual machines inside a computer: lifecycle, media, snapshots
- `watch` — Linux inotify file-change streams with replay history

# `agent` — In-computer AI coding agent over HTTP

## Purpose

The `agent` kit exposes the in-computer AI agent as a typed namespace: create a chat session, send a prompt, stream the turn (tool calls, gates, output), then confirm/answer/cancel as the agent works. services — `sessions` (with `sessions.turns`), `bots`, `definitions`, `models`, `providers`, `skills` (with `skills.hub`), `memory`, `github`, `workflows`, `tools`, `hooks`, `mcp`, `settings`, `loops`, `logs` (with `hoody agent logs export`), `jobs`, `gates`, `changes`, `headless`, `todos`, `usage` (usage statistics), plus the namespace's own calls (`whoami`, the `login` token bootstrap, `pause` and `resume`). Session tasks live under `sessions.tasks`.

## When to use

- **Drive the agent programmatically** — create a session, prompt it, and consume the turn: `hoody agent sessions create` → stream the turn for live tool/gate/output events (per surface — see the streaming note under Quirks), or `hoody agent sessions turns run` for one blocking call → resolve gates with `hoody agent gates approve` / `hoody agent gates deny` / `hoody agent gates answer` → `hoody agent sessions turns cancel` to interrupt.
- **Inspect or configure the agent** — list `models` (`hoody agent models list` / `hoody agent models get`; the Jev decision-model catalogue is the separate `hoody agent jev models list`) and `hoody agent providers list` (configure providers via `hoody agent providers auth default set` / `hoody agent providers apikey set` / `hoody agent providers oauth start`); switch a session's active model with `hoody agent sessions model set`, browse/install `skills`, read/edit `memory`, manage `workflows`, `hooks`, `definitions` (named agent profiles), and `tools` — both the sessionless catalogue/registry (`hoody agent tools list` / `hoody agent tools readonly list` / `hoody agent tools get`, and `hoody agent tools run` (blocks, returns the result; `hoody agent tools run --stream` returns the one-shot result over SSE frames instead, not a per-token stream) / `hoody agent tools start` (returns `{ job_id }`, poll `jobs`) to invoke a tool with no session — read-only by default, a mutating tool needs `allow_mutations: true` or a confirmed re-issue) and the per-session surface (`hoody agent sessions tools list` for a session's *effective* tool set, `hoody agent sessions tools mcp list`, and `hoody agent sessions tools run`). Unlike the sessionless `hoody agent tools run`, a per-session run executes against the session's *frozen* realm/computer/cwd/tool-mode and claims the session's single serial turn slot — so it returns 409 `turn_in_flight` while a turn is running, 409 `gate_parked` while a gate is open, and 404 `tool_not_found` if the tool is not in that session's effective list; whether a mutating tool may run is decided by the live session's own tool mode and confirmation settings (the `allow_mutations` escape hatch is sessionless-only).
- **One-shot non-interactive runs** — a headless run (`POST /api/v1/agent/headless/runs`) runs the full agent loop once over a throwaway session (see workflow 7 for the per-surface form: an async job or an SSE stream).
- **GitHub from inside the agent** — first establish an account with `hoody agent github auth start` (a GitHub device flow → poll `hoody agent github auth poll`) or `hoody agent github auth login --github-token <token>` (a PAT, persisted directly), then `hoody agent github auth status` to confirm; once an account is active, `hoody agent github repos clone` / `hoody agent github commits create` (and `hoody agent github status` / `hoody agent github branches list` / `hoody agent github repos list` / `hoody agent github prs create` / `hoody agent github sync`) for repo operations the agent performs in-computer.

## When NOT to use

- Want an interactive UI, not the API? The agent's own TUI opens at its `agent-1` URL or a terminal link with `agent=true`; in a terminal, `hoody hub` opens the Hub. This namespace is the HTTP control surface beside them.
- Raw shell / command exec → `terminal` (PTY) or `exec` (one-shot). File I/O → `files`. The agent runs these as tools internally; call them directly when you don't need the LLM.
- Account-level resources (computers, billing, realms) → `api`.

## Prerequisites

- Computer with the `agent` kit running; capability URL.
- At least one usable model provider before prompting: one with a stored API key, a stored OAuth login, or passwordless access (the shipped default agent is pinned to a passwordless model). `hoody agent providers list` and `hoody agent models list` list the CATALOGUE, which is populated whether or not anything is configured; `hoody agent providers auth status` reports whether a provider is actually usable (`ready`, with `api_key_stored`, `oauth_stored` and `no_auth_ready` behind it).
- A session id from `hoody agent sessions create` for every prompt/gate/cancel call.

## Capability URL

→ See `SKILL-CLI.md § Proxy URLs`.

**Reaching a service you host on a computer port** (any port, any namespace):

- `https://{projectId}-{computerId}-http-<port>.{node}.computers.hoody.com` — proxy speaks HTTP to `<port>` on the computer's network address. Bind `0.0.0.0:<port>`, which always works; a loopback-only listener is also reached on default computers.
- `https://{projectId}-{computerId}-https-<port>.{node}.computers.hoody.com` — proxy speaks HTTPS to `<port>` on the computer's network address (target needs TLS, bound to `0.0.0.0:<port>` too).

Edge is always `https://`. No alias, firewall edit, or proxy registration needed; capability-token gates still apply.

## Common workflows

### 1. Prompt a session and stream the turn

`hoody agent sessions create` (returns a session id) → stream the turn with `{ text }` to receive live events (tool calls, gates, output deltas) — see the streaming note under Quirks for the supported per-surface method (SDK helper / HTTP SSE route / CLI command) → resolve any gate as it arrives → turn ends.

### 2. One-shot synchronous prompt

`hoody agent sessions create` → `hoody agent sessions turns run` with `{ text }` — waits for the turn to end, a gate that needs a person, or the server deadline (290 seconds by default). A clean turn returns `{status:"done", session_id, turn_id}` with no reply text; check `status`, because a failed, cancelled or quit turn answers `error` (with the error `event`), `canceled` or `quit`. A turn that parks on a gate returns `{pending_gate, turn_id}`. When the deadline passes first the answer is `503 service_unavailable` with `details.turn_id` and `details.turn_running: true`: the turn is NOT cancelled, so follow it with `hoody agent sessions turns get` (or the stream) instead of prompting again. Read the reply with `hoody agent sessions transcript get`. Best for short, non-interactive prompts where you don't need streamed events.

### 3. Resolve gates mid-turn

While a prompt streams, the agent may pause for human input: a confirmation gate → `hoody agent gates approve` / `hoody agent gates deny`; an open question → `hoody agent gates answer` (to get a helper model to DRAFT an answer for a parked question call `hoody agent gates suggest` — it does NOT answer the gate and needs a parked lead question gate (otherwise `409 no_pending_gate`; a helper's gate does not count): it dispatches an async job (HTTP 202) whose suggestion arrives via `hoody agent jobs result get` and an `event.question_suggestion` on the session stream — only one assist may be in flight per session — and the real answer still goes through `hoody agent gates answer`; for unattended runs arm `hoody agent sessions autoreply update` (a self-driving auto-user loop that answers questions only during its own rounds, so arming it does not resolve a question an ordinary prompt already parked: answer that with `hoody agent gates answer`; it also withholds write-class actions unless you opt in with `allow_writes: true`, either on the arm call or later via `hoody agent sessions autoreply writes enable`)). The gate identity to echo is the ENVELOPE-level `gate {id, generation, type}` that the stream frame parking the gate carries beside `seq` / `incarnation` / `event`. The `event.confirm_request` payload also has a numeric `gate_id`, but that is the daemon's id space and is never the value to echo. The answer body for a question gate: the envelope's gate id as `gate_id` (optionally its `generation`), then **answer** (or **text**, used when **answer** is blank) for a single question; for a batch (`event.user_question` carrying `questions[]`), `answers` maps each `questions[].id` to its answer text, for example `{"gate_id":"<gate.id>","answers":{"<questions[].id>":"yes"}}`. A body with no `answer`, no `text` and no `answers` is `400 bad_request` and the question stays parked. The `question_id` on `event.user_question` is a diagnostic number, not a body field. Echoing a wrong/stale `gate_id`/`generation`, or answering when nothing is parked, returns 409 (`no_pending_gate` / `stale_gate` / `gate_already_answered` / `gate_type_mismatch`). A retry of a question answer that names the gate just resolved with the same answer (a lost 200) gets `200` with `replayed: true` and the original acknowledgement, while another answer to that gate is `409 gate_already_answered`. For `hoody agent gates approve` / `hoody agent gates deny`, a decision naming a gate that already ended is `409 gate_already_resolved` (with its recorded outcome), and one naming a gate whose decision is still being applied is `409 gate_decision_pending`: retry naming the gate to learn the outcome. On a session whose approval policy is `always` and whose approver lease was ever minted (`hoody agent sessions approverlease claim`, or the lease handed back by a create or attach that asserted `always`), EVERY decision — `hoody agent gates approve` / `hoody agent gates deny`, and the confirmed re-issue of a gated `hoody agent sessions tools run` — must carry the current lease capability in the `X-Hoody-Approver-Lease` request header. (CLI: `--approver-lease`.) Without it the decision is refused `409 approver_lease_required`, a capability that does not verify is `409 approver_lease_invalid`, and an expired one is `approver_lease_expired` until a holder acquires again. Interrupt a running turn with `hoody agent sessions turns cancel`. Tear the session down: `hoody agent sessions close` removes it from the live map; `hoody agent sessions delete --id <id>` always erases the persisted record too (the CLI has no keep-the-record form; re-attach with `hoody agent sessions create --attach-session-id <id>` works only after `sessions close`). To roll a session back without tearing it down, `hoody agent sessions trim` with `{ turn_idx }` truncates conversation history to (and including) that turn index.

### 4. Pick a model / provider

`hoody agent providers list` to list the catalogued providers (and `hoody agent providers auth status` to check that one is `ready`: a stored credential or passwordless access), `hoody agent models list` to list the catalogued models, then `hoody agent sessions model set` to bind a model to a session before prompting — SYNCHRONOUS: the response reports the actual outcome ({status:'ok', model, persisted} on success; structured 409/422 errors while busy or for an unconstructable spec). For a native session, the default `scope: "agent"` switches the session and TRIES to rewrite the `model:` line of the chat agent's highest-precedence on-disk file (project before home; an embedded-only agent in a scoped realm gets a new copy in that realm's profile layer). That pin applies to later sessions resolving that file: it is per profile layer, not global. That save is best-effort, so only `persisted: true` confirms the repin — `persisted: false` means the session switched but future sessions keep the old pin. With `scope: "session"` (`--scope session`), the switch affects only this session and leaves the agent file alone; `persisted` then says whether the session record was saved. A Claude Code (delegated) session's switch is always session-scoped, takes a Claude alias or model id, and applies from its next turn; it does not rewrite an agent file. PRECEDENCE: the agent's frontmatter `model` is the DEFAULT for a session that does not request one; an explicit model on create (`hoody agent sessions create --model <spec>`), or this live `hoody agent sessions model set`, OVERRIDES that pin for the session — create is session-scoped and does not rewrite the agent, for a native session, this live switch repins the agent file it resolves with the default scope (see above). The shipped default agent ships pinned, so its pin is the out-of-the-box default until an explicit model is chosen (an explicit model together with `attach` is rejected 400, because a resumed session keeps its model; with `backend: "acp"` the model is the Claude Code model: a Claude alias such as `opus`, `sonnet` or `haiku`, or a Claude model id. Any other model is `422 model_unavailable` with `details.reason: not_claude`). Each session has further per-session knobs (all session-scoped PATCHes; while a gate is parked, `hoody agent sessions effort set` and `hoody agent sessions agent set` answer 200 with `deferred: true`, and the change is dropped, not queued: send it again once the turn has ended): `hoody agent sessions effort set` (`{ effort }` — `low|medium|high|xhigh|max`, or `""` for the model default), `hoody agent sessions verbosity set` (`{ level }` — `normal|concise|terse|minimal`), `hoody agent sessions hoodyenv enable` / `hoody agent sessions hoodyenv disable` (turn injection of the `HOODY_*` shell-env contract for the bash tool on or off), and `hoody agent sessions agent set` (`{ agent }` — bind a named profile from `definitions` (`hoody agent definitions list`); `bot`, `script-writer` and `github-installer` are refused `400 bad_request` (a Bot runs `bot`, and the other two are fixed at session start: a session started on one cannot switch away)).

To use a model from an endpoint that is not in the catalogue (anything that speaks the OpenAI Chat Completions, OpenAI Responses or Anthropic Messages API from a public HTTPS address, such as a model server you run yourself or a company gateway), add it as a **custom provider** first. `hoody agent providers create` takes `--id`, `--endpoint` (the base URL) and one `--models model=<name>` per model, then `hoody agent providers apikey set --id <id> --api-key <key>` stores its key (a key never goes in the create command), and its models are `<model_prefix>/<model>` wherever a model is chosen: `hoody agent sessions create --model <spec>`. `hoody agent providers update` changes it and `hoody agent providers delete` removes it; `api_key_removed` in the result says whether its stored key was removed too. The change applies at once, with no restart: new sessions, model switches and Jev see it, and an open session on one of its models picks it up before its next turn. `id` is 1-40 lowercase letters, digits or inner hyphens and cannot change later; `model_prefix` is the `id` unless given, and must equal it; `wire_format` is `chat_completions` (default), `responses` or `messages`, and `auth_scheme` follows it (`bearer`, or `x-api-key` for `messages`). Built-in providers refuse update and delete (`409 provider_builtin`), as does a provider defined in a project's providers file (`409 provider_not_managed`). See Examples for the full run.

### 5. Skills, memory, todos, workflows, agents

- **Skills** — `hoody agent skills list` (each carries an enabled + trust state), `hoody agent skills hub install` / `hoody agent skills hub search` / `hoody agent skills hub preview` to find and install from the hub. A newly installed/imported skill must be trusted before its code runs — `hoody agent skills trust` is the gate (identify the skill by `root_dir`+`rel_dir`; `hoody agent skills untrust` takes the trust back); `hoody agent skills enable` / `hoody agent skills disable` enable or disable by `name`. Both `hoody agent skills trust` (which grants arbitrary code-execution trust) and `hoody agent skills hub install` (which writes arbitrary skill code to disk) take effect immediately over this namespace: there is no confirmation step, and no privilege beyond ordinary access to the kit is required, so an autonomous caller can silently trust and install skill code. Add your own confirmation before exposing these to one.
- **Memory** — `hoody agent memory search` for hybrid recall (BM25 + vector + graph) and `hoody agent memory items list` to enumerate by `project`; `hoody agent memory items create` / `hoody agent memory items update` / `hoody agent memory items delete` to write; `hoody agent memory graph get` for the relation graph (or `hoody agent memory items get` to read one record by `id`). `hoody agent memory enable` / `hoody agent memory disable` are the memory capture/privacy switch — they persist `features.memory` and flip the live store — and `hoody agent memory flush` forces the store's durability barrier; none of the three is admin-gated. Memory is project-scoped (pass `project`). Memory reads and item writes accept `X-Hoody-Realm` or `?realm=` to select `global` or a realm id (in the SDK, pass `agentRealm` in the method's options); omitted, the agent's current realm is used. A realm this login does not serve returns `404 not_found`; an agent pinned to one realm refuses another with `400 realm_scope_unsupported`. If the selected realm's memory is not connected, the request returns `503 service_unavailable` with `Retry-After` and does not connect it. `hoody agent memory consolidate` is a guarded write: it needs a single-use intent from `hoody agent memory writeintents create`; see Common errors. `hoody agent memory search` / `hoody agent memory graph get` also return `503 store_unavailable` while the store is still warming — retry rather than treating it as an empty result.
- **Todos** — `hoody agent todos list` / `hoody agent todos create` to file; then `hoody agent todos triage` (LLM inbox pass), `hoody agent todos claim` / `hoody agent todos release`, `hoody agent todos start` (dispatch a background orchestrator — returns `{job_id, session_id}`), `hoody agent todos cancel` to abort an in-flight run, and `hoody agent todos proposals approve` / `hoody agent todos proposals deny` to resolve a proposed run — approve is NOT inert: it spawns a background worker session equivalent to `hoody agent todos start` (a J-class autonomous run that spends model budget), while `hoody agent todos proposals deny` spawns nothing — plus `hoody agent todos snooze` / `hoody agent todos archive`. To move a todo between states (`inbox`, `ready`, `blocked`, `review`, `done`, `dropped`) or edit its fields, `hoody agent todos update` applies a CAS-guarded patch / `state` transition (`in_progress` is entered only by `hoody agent todos claim` / `hoody agent todos start`; `hoody agent todos update` refuses it, and an unknown state is rejected) — read the todo's OWN `revision` with `hoody agent todos get` and pass it back (`hoody agent todos revision get` is a change cursor filtered by realm and account visibility, NOT the per-todo CAS token; a stale value → `409 todo_conflict`); a stale revision is rejected (409). `hoody agent todos archive` is not terminal — `hoody agent todos archived purge` permanently and irreversibly deletes archived todos of the selected realm that were archived more than 90 days ago (and those with a missing or invalid archive time); a read-only todo from before the computer rename is kept; no confirmation gate, treat as destructive. Mind the comment split: `hoody agent todos comments create` (`/messages`, plural) only appends a comment, whereas `hoody agent todos messages send` (`/message`, singular) ALSO kicks an orchestrator turn — a budget-spending LLM run that returns `{job_id}` — so use the plural form for a plain note. The `job_id` returned by `hoody agent todos start`, `hoody agent todos messages send` and `hoody agent todos triage` completes as `succeeded` the moment the dispatch is accepted; it records the dispatch only, not the worker's outcome. Follow the todo itself (`hoody agent todos get`, its state and timeline) rather than polling that job. Note `hoody agent todos start` / `hoody agent todos triage` / `hoody agent todos proposals approve` are J-class autonomous runs with NO confirmation gate on the RPC (reaching the RPC is itself treated as the human approval; that denial lives only on the model-facing `run_todo` *tool*), so calling them from automation silently dispatches a real LLM run — gate them in your own caller.
- **Workflows** — `hoody agent workflows list` / `hoody agent workflows get` / `hoody agent workflows set` / `hoody agent workflows delete` / `hoody agent workflows hide` / `hoody agent workflows unhide` manage saved definitions; `hoody agent sessions workflows start` dispatches one onto a live session and returns a JOB, not a run (optionally seed the run with a `{ prompt }` body — input text fed to the workflow). `hoody agent workflows set` takes the whole definition as `definition`; a small definition that saves is `{"entry_point":{"id":"check"},"steps":{"check":{"type":"bash","command":"echo hello"}}}` (`steps` is a non-empty object keyed by step id; this example uses a `bash` step with a `command` and ends after that step because it has no `next_steps`). Save it as `workflow.json` and pass `--definition @workflow.json` — poll `hoody agent jobs get`, checking both `status` and `run_id`: once `run_id` populates (null during the brief dispatch window), track the run via `hoody agent workflows runs list` / `hoody agent workflows runs get` and stop it with `hoody agent workflows runs cancel`; a dispatch the agent refuses (a missing required input, a blocking hook, no configured model) ends the job as failed with `run_id` still null, so read its result and the session stream: no run exists to track or cancel; feed a running workflow with `hoody agent workflows messages send` (`{ text }`). Run events flow on the owning session's stream, not a per-run bus.
- **Bots** — `hoody agent bots create` opens a long-lived assistant that delegates work to sessions on computers; post to it with `hoody agent bots messages send` (HTTP 202; a busy Bot queues the message) rather than prompting its session, and see Examples for the full create, message, follow, forget, delete run. Replace its limits with `hoody agent bots guardrails set --id <id> --guardrails <guardrails>` (empty clears them): the Bot reads them before its next message and delegates opened afterwards receive them in their first prompt, while delegates already open keep theirs. `allowed_computers` and `allowed_agents` restrict the delegates it opens next (empty means any) and `yolo: true` (default false) asks delegates to approve tool calls automatically. Check `yolo_unapplied` in `hoody agent bots get`: `pending` means a delegate has not confirmed the change yet and it is sent again; `refused` means that delegate's approval policy does not allow YOLO, so it keeps asking for approvals and the change is not sent again until `yolo` changes. `hoody agent bots logs stream` and `hoody agent bots logs get` carry finished rows only; for live reply text, thinking and tool calls follow the Bot's `session_id` (from `hoody agent bots get`, it changes after `hoody agent bots reset`) with `hoody agent sessions stream`, and do not answer questions on that session whose `frame_request.kind` starts with `bot.`, because the Bot runtime answers them. To stop only the Bot's running turn, cancel its `session_id` with `hoody agent sessions turns cancel --id <session_id> --turn-id <turn_id>` (there is no `bots` command for it), naming the `turn_id` that `hoody agent bots get` shows while `turn_running` is true.
- **Share a Bot through a public URL** — a Bot URL, `https://<label>.hoody.bot`, lets a person with no Hoody account talk to one of your Bots with a named key (`hbk_…`) you hand out. It belongs to your account, not to the agent kit: `hoody boturls create` and `hoody boturls keys create` manage it, and `hoody boturls ask <url> "…"` is the caller side. You name the Bot by the `realm`, `id` and `uid` that `hoody agent bots get` returns. A Bot has one Bot URL at most, a deleted and recreated Bot has a new `uid` that the URL does not follow (`repoint` it), and everyone holding a key shares one conversation with the Bot. Example 4 runs the whole flow (create, key, call, rotate, panic); the `## Bot URLs` section of the appendix is the reference for the doors, the caller client and the errors.
- **Audio / voice** — the kit speaks and listens through the speech models it lists. `hoody agent audio models list --capability tts` or `hoody agent audio models list --capability stt` lists the text-to-speech and speech-to-text models with their formats, rates, languages and whether their provider has a key; `hoody agent audio voices list --model <spec>` lists a model's voices (omit `--model` for the voices of every available model except the Hoody AI relay ones, which are listed only when named with `--model`). `hoody agent audio speech create --input "<text>" --response-format mp3 --out-file hello.mp3` speaks the text (at most 4096 characters) and writes the audio as one file; the streamed form of that call (SSE frames of base64 audio) has no CLI command, since a terminal can neither play nor show them. Transcription takes a `multipart/form-data` upload, which has no CLI command: post the recording over HTTP to the kit URL (`hoody open agent --url` prints it) with `curl -sS -X POST "${K%/}/api/v1/agent/audio/transcriptions" -F file=@recording.wav` (`-F language=…`, `-F model=…`, `-F prompt=…`, `-F response_format=…` optional; wav or mp3, at most 16 MiB and 600 seconds) to get `{ text }` with the default `response_format` `json` (`text`: the plain transcript; `verbose_json`: `text` plus `language`, `duration` and `segments` when the model gives them), or `…/transcriptions/stream` for the SSE form (`transcript.text.delta`, then `transcript.text.done` with the whole `text`), wav and mp3 only, for models with partial results. A capability the model lacks (a format, `instructions`, a `speed`) is refused `400` before any paid call; `response_format` is `mp3`, `wav` or `pcm` (16-bit little-endian mono, no header; omitted: `wav`, or `mp3` when the model gives no wav, and on a stream `pcm`, else `mp3`). Some transcription models also take webm, ogg, m4a or flac on the non-streaming call (the model's `opaque_formats`): Hoody passes those on undecoded, does not verify their duration, and bills the provider's reported duration or the model's maximum when none is reported. Every speech call is billed, a stream included, so do not replay a stream automatically; a failure before the first frame is an ordinary JSON error with its status, after it an `error` frame, and a `: ping` comment arrives every 25 s. `X-Hoody-Realm` (or `?realm=`, `--agent-realm`) names the realm the call is billed to; omitted, the agent's current realm. The cwd, config-dir and computer headers are refused `400 realm_scope_unsupported`.
- **Spoken messages to a Bot** — `POST /api/v1/agent/bots/{id}/messages/audio` over HTTP (`curl -F file=@recording.wav -F language=en`; a multipart upload has no CLI command, so use HTTP or the SDK) transcribes one recording (wav or mp3, at most 16 MiB and 600 seconds) and queues the transcript as a message to the Bot exactly like `hoody agent bots messages send`: `202 { message_id, state: 'posted' | 'queued' | 'dropped', turn_id?, transcript }`. `dropped` means the Bot dropped the message before posting it and never will post it (`reason` says why); that key keeps answering `dropped`, so send the recording again under a new key. Audio with no speech in it is answered `200 { no_speech: true }` and nothing is queued or billed. Send an `Idempotency-Key` on anything you may retry: once the message is admitted, the same key with the same audio, the same `language` and the Bot's same `speech.stt_model` and `speech.stt_prompt` returns the same `message_id` without transcribing again (a replay of a finished one has no `transcript`; a retry that waited on one still running gets it), and the same key with any of those changed is `422`, even for the same recording. A transcription that failed or was refused stores nothing, so a retry with that key transcribes again; a recording with no speech in it is answered `no_speech` each time, without a transcription. At most 4 recordings per Bot are transcribed at once (`503 speech_busy` past it); a request repeating the key of one still running waits for it (`429 speech_busy` when too many wait); `409 bot_deleted` or `bot_reset` means the Bot was deleted or reset before the recording was admitted. The Bot's `speech` settings (`tts_model`, `stt_model`, `voice`, `language`, `speed`, `speak_wakes`, `speak_gates`) choose the models and voice used for its spoken messages and replies.
- **Talk to a Bot by voice (WebSocket)** — `GET /api/v1/agent/bots/{id}/voice` upgrades to a WebSocket (request it with `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol: hoody.voice.v1`) that carries the user's speech to the Bot and the Bot's spoken replies back (from a terminal, `hoody agent bots voice connect --id <bot>` records the microphone and plays the reply through the audio programs already installed, push-to-talk by default, `--mode vad` for hands-free; `--in-file question.wav --once` sends one 16-bit PCM mono WAV at 8000, 16000, 24000 or 48000 Hz and exits 0 when the answer arrived, its turn did not fail and its speech did not fail, else 1 with the reason (2 when the flags conflict or no computer is selected); `--audio-output none` asks for text-only replies; `--doctor` prints the readiness check below with the local audio checks, and the check has no command of its own). The readiness check behind `--doctor` answers 200 either way with `{ ready, speak, stt, tts, max_utterance_secs, diag_id? }`: `stt` and `tts` (`null` with `speak=false`) each carry `ok` and `model` (plus `language` or `voice`), and when `ok` is false also `code`, `reason`, `message`, `retryable` and, when known, `retry_after_secs` and `diag_id`. It follows the inference path (the Bot's own model, else the agent's `audio.stt_model` and `audio.tts_model` settings, else the Hoody AI voice relay when the audio setting `relay_default` is on; then capability, voice and language, then key), runs no inference, bills nothing and takes at most 6 s; `ready` is not a promise that the provider will answer. `require=stt`, `require=tts` or `require=stt,tts` on the voice URL runs the same check before the upgrade and refuses it `400 bad_request` when every failure is a voice or language the model does not offer, else `503 speech_unavailable`, with the check's result in `details` (messages may be shortened and the echoed model, voice and language values removed to fit the error's size limit; `details` is omitted if the reduced result still does not fit); a refused check takes nothing over; omitted, nothing is checked; `require=tts` with `speak=false` is `400`. `speak=false` gives text-only replies: no speech is made, every `reply.final` has `spoken: false`, nothing is billed for synthesis (speech-to-text still is), and the `session` frame shows `speak: false`. An agent supports `require`, `speak` and the check when `GET /api/v1/agent/version` lists the capability `bot_voice_check` with `supported` and `available` true. `mode` is fixed for the connection (default `vad`); in `ptt` mode only audio between `ptt.down` and `ptt.up` counts and other audio is dropped. One utterance is at most 60 seconds, or the speech-to-text model's limit when lower. Binary frames from the client are input audio: one byte `0x00`, a big-endian unsigned 32-bit sequence number, then 20 to 200 ms of audio in `in_format` (`pcm16` default, `pcmu`, `pcma`) at `in_rate` (8000, 16000 default, 24000 or 48000); binary frames from the agent are output audio: one byte `0x01`, a big-endian unsigned 32-bit output number, a big-endian unsigned 32-bit sample offset, then 16-bit little-endian PCM at `out_rate` (default 24000). Text frames are JSON objects with a `type`: the client sends `input.commit`, `ptt.down` / `ptt.up` (`mode=ptt`; the default `vad` lets the agent hear when the user starts and stops), `output.cancel`, `playback.mark` (with `play_lead=true`, at least every 500 ms while playing), `own_gate.decide` / `own_gate.answer`, `text` and `ping`; the agent sends `session` first, then `vad.start` / `vad.end`, `transcript.partial` / `transcript.final`, `reply.provisional` / `reply.invalidate` / `reply.final` / `reply.diverged`, `output.start` / `output.end` / `output.stop`, `cancel.result`, `gate.announced`, `own_gate.pending` / `own_gate.resolved`, `busy`, `error`, `takeover` and `pong`. A spoken message counts once the Bot's log shows it; only replies to this connection's own messages are spoken (plus the Bot's own replies with `speak_wakes`), and every reply's final text still arrives in `reply.final` (at most 64 KiB: a longer text is cut and `truncated` is true; the whole text is in the Bot's log). Voice never answers a delegate's approval or question: answer it on screen or by typing. One connection controls a Bot's voice at a time, over this route, the Realtime route or a phone call: a second is refused `409 voice_busy` unless it asks `takeover=true`, which closes the first (it receives `takeover`, close 1000). `reply.final` carries `own: true` when its turn answers a message sent on this connection, `false` when it does not, and no `own` when the connection cannot tell; `own` is about this connection only: a new connection starts at the next event, so a reconnect that misses the turn start gets no `own` on that reply (not `own: false`), and when it is absent match the reply's `turn_id` and your `message_id` in the Bot's log. A speech failure carries `error { code, reason?, message, diag_id?, retryable, retry_after_secs? }`: on `transcript.final` when it `failed` or was `rejected` `stt_suspect` (the outer `failed` value is unchanged; branch on `error.code` when present), on `reply.final` when `reason` is `tts_failed` or `tts_incomplete`, and on an `error` frame with code `service_unavailable` when the speech service failed while a gate announcement was spoken (at most once per code and reason per connection; the connection stays open; an announcement stopped for the daily speech limit, or silenced because speech output is off, sends no error frame). `message` says what happened and what to do next; `diag_id` names the failure in the agent's log. A `pcm16` frame of an odd byte length, a sequence gap, or audio faster than 1.5 times real time over 2 s counts as lost: the open utterance ends `rejected: frame_loss` and the connection stays open. The connection closes 1000 when the client closes it, after 10 minutes without a frame from the client (the Bot's output does not count; send `ping`), on takeover or when the Bot is deleted or suspended; 1001 when the Bot is stopped (as when the agent shuts down); 1002 without the subprotocol; 1008 for a malformed frame, text frames faster than 50 a second once the burst of 100 (the bucket starts full) is used up, an input frame outside 20 to 200 ms or a `playback.mark` past the audio sent; 1009 for a frame over 64 KiB; 1011 when a write fails, the agent runs out of voice memory, or on an internal error (a client that does not read gets no close frame; the connection just ends). The Bot's own approvals and questions (`own_gate.decide` / `own_gate.answer`) report their outcome in `own_gate.resolved` (`applied`, `resolved`, `stale`, `unavailable`, `not_offered`, `no_pending_gate`, `stale_gate`, `gate_cancelled` or `decision_unconfirmed`), never as an HTTP status.
- **Talk to a Bot with an OpenAI Realtime client (WebSocket)** — `GET /api/v1/agent/bots/{id}/realtime` upgrades to a WebSocket that speaks the OpenAI Realtime protocol (GA event names), so an off-the-shelf Realtime client library talks to the Bot (SDK and HTTP only; no CLI command). The client sends `session.update`, `input_audio_buffer.append` / `.commit` / `.clear`, `conversation.item.create` / `.delete` / `.retrieve` / `.truncate`, `response.create` and `response.cancel`; the agent answers with the matching server events (`session.created` first). Input audio is `audio/pcm` (24000 Hz, 16-bit little-endian, the default), `audio/pcmu` or `audio/pcma` (8000 Hz); output audio follows the session's output format. With `server_vad` the agent hears when the user starts and stops speaking and answers on its own; without turn detection the client commits and asks with `response.create`. A user item reaches the Bot once, by its id, and the Bot never forgets an id it has seen, so a client replaying its history on reconnect does not resend an old item; at the Bot's limit (`realtime_items` on the Bot) a new item is refused and the connection closed. An event that would change an item already sent (deleting, truncating or editing a user item waiting for a response) closes the connection with 1008; so do a binary or non-JSON frame, a frame over 1 MiB, control events faster than 50 a second once the burst of 100 (the bucket starts full) is used up, and input audio faster than 1.5 times real time. The same one-controller rule applies: `409 voice_busy` unless `takeover=true`. A WebSocket upgrade of the Bot's own OpenAI base URL plus `/realtime` (`…/api/v1/agent/bots/<realm>/<bot>/v1/realtime`, the `urls.openai` of `hoody agent bots get` plus `/realtime`) opens the same connection for a Realtime client that only takes a base URL, with the same `?takeover=true`.
- **A phone call as the Bot's voice** — `GET /api/v1/agent/bots/{id}/twilio` is the WebSocket URL for Twilio's `<Connect><Stream>` instruction: one Twilio Media Stream becomes the Bot's voice controller (no CLI command: the peer is a phone call's media stream, not a terminal; follow the call's effect with `hoody agent bots logs stream --id <bot>`). Audio is μ-law at 8000 Hz, mono; Twilio's `connected`, `start`, `media`, `mark`, `stop` and `dtmf` events are taken as Twilio documents them.
